title: The Most Annoying Employee I’ve Ever Had 2026
author: Jeff Matlow
source: thebestleadershipnewsletter.com (The Best Leadership Newsletter Ever), September 28,
summary: Jeff Matlow compares Apple's Siri, which merely transcribes the words you say, with the dictation tool Wispr Flow, which learns how you talk and infers what you mean, and turns the contrast into a model of two kinds of employees. "Siri employees" follow instructions literally and leave the manager explaining, checking and redoing the work indefinitely. "Wispr employees" learn how their boss thinks, absorb every correction and need less direction over time. His claim is that people are promoted not for following instructions well but for making the manager's life easier. He then turns the lens on the reader, who is also someone's employee, and argues that great work comes from learning the person giving the instructions rather than demanding they be spelled out perfectly. The piece is brief and uses a product anecdote, but the leadership argument is clear.
points: Employees who execute literal instructions create double work for managers, who must explain the task and then review and correct the result every time.
The best employees learn how their manager thinks and what matters to them, so each correction improves later output instead of repeating the same errors.
Promotion tends to follow trust with complicated work, which comes from making the manager's life easier rather than from following instructions precisely.
Leaders are also followers: the same test applies to how you respond to incomplete or hurried instructions from your own boss, board or client.
The difference between good and great is not how well you listen but how much you learn about the person you are listening to.
quotes: If I say something wrong, Siri transcribes it wrong. If I correct myself halfway through a sentence, Siri types the mistake, the correction and all the gobbledygook in between.
I’m trusting software to decide what I meant instead of what I said. And it does a great job.
Most employees operate like Siri. You give them instructions and they translate your literal words into a literal task. It’s literally annoying.
Siri employees aren’t the ones who get promoted first. They’re the ones people stop trusting with complicated work.

They figure out how you think and what matters to you. They pay attention to how you make decisions and what you mean when you say something that probably made a heckuva lot of sense inside your head but not so much when it came out of your mouth.
Every time you give an instruction to a Siri employee, you’re doing twice the work. First you explain what you want. Then you check it, correct it or redo it.
Because if you need everything spelled out perfectly before you can do great work, you’re not being careful. You’re being Siri.
